title: Using CRISPR to modify the genome of the human fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans
description: The focus of the lab is to understand how the pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans is able to infect, survive, and cause disease in mammalian hosts such as humans. One mechanism we utilize is gene editing in Cryptococcus using CRISPR technology.

title: Ticks as vectors of disease
description: Assessment of ticks as vector for One Health pathogens of disease

title: How much does vacuum pressure impact destruction of pathogens during sous vide cooking?
description: Sous vide is the cooking of vacuum packaged meat in a water bath. It has become increasingly popular with the availability and affordability of home cook-level heating devices. However, there is a big difference between meat that is commercially vacuum sealed, and meat placed into a storage bag and squeezing out the air, and it may have implications on the ability to control foodborne pathogens. Potentially, cooking without the benefit of vacuum sealing may change the relative lethality of sous vide cooking, but there is just no data to suggest if, or to what extent, this may be true.

title: Using Metagenomics to Detect and Identify Pathogens Affecting Plant and Animal Health
description: This project introduces students to the use of metagenomics and genomic technologies for identifying pathogens associated with plant and animal diseases. The student will work with the research team at Virginia Tech’s (Meta)Genomics-Based Pathogen Identification Center for Animal and Plant Disease Diagnostics, Biosecurity, and Pandemic Prevention to explore how DNA and RNA sequencing can detect bacteria, fungi, viruses, and other microorganisms directly from biological samples. Depending on the project stage, activities may include sample and data organization, basic laboratory procedures such as nucleic acid extractions, sequencing library preparation and sequencing. The student will gain hands-on experience with modern approaches used in metagenomics disease diagnostics, surveillance, and pathogen discovery.

title: Determining the First Amino Acid Sequence of Proteins Unencoded By The Genome
description: When a ribosome stalls, a quality-control system extends the trapped protein with "CAT tails" — amino acids added with no genetic template. Because these sequences come from no gene and appear as heterogeneous smears, none has ever been sequenced, and no antibody against them exists. Using a reporter we engineered to make CAT tails of a single, defined length, this project will purify these tails from yeast and determine their amino acid sequence for the first time. That sequence will let us build the first anti-CAT-tail antibody and identify the proteins cells naturally tail.

title: Bacteriophages of the soybean symbiont Bradyrhizobium diazoefficiens
description: Soybean is an important crop and the most common source for vegetable oil. The symbiotic bacterium Bradyrhizobium diazoefficiens is found in leguminous root nodules, where it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and ultimately stimulates soybean growth. Bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria, are the most abundant biological entity on earth and important factors in shaping ecosystems including during bacteria-host interactions. However, very little is known about bacteriophages infecting symbiotic rhizobia. This is particularly true for the soybean symbiont and only a few Bradyrhizobium phages have been described. We will isolate B. diazoefficiens phages from soybean nodules and characterize their interaction with their host.

title: Finding novel phages from the environment
description: Bacteriophages (phages) are viruses that specifically target bacteria. Often phages are of interest because of their ability to kill pathogenic bacteria, however they can also coexist with non-pathogenic bacteria including those that naturally reside in the gut microbiome. Little is known about the importance of these phages and a major limitation is that we have a limited availability of characterized phages that target these non-pathogenic bacteria.

title: TEAM Malawi
description: Students enrolled in this section of IDS 4994 will leverage the Biodesign Process (Figure 1, below) to identify and invent solutions to high-priority projects in sub-Saharan Africa. All of these projects are underpinned by the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with a focus on SDG #3: Good Health & Wellbeing, SDG #9: Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure, and SDG #10: Reduced Inequalities. Students will be assigned to one of these projects based on alignment with skills and interests.

title: Examining the variation of microplastic type and abundance over seasons and sites within Watamu Marine National Park and Reserve, Kenya
description: Microplastic pollution is an increasing threat to marine ecosystems, yet little is known about contamination in protected coastal areas of Kenya. This project provides the first assessment of microplastic abundance and composition along sandy shorelines within Watamu Marine National Park. Samples were collected across five sampling periods in 2021–2022 using standardized transect and quadrat methods, and microplastics were extracted, classified, measured, and enumerated. The student will help complete data organization, quality control, statistical analyses, and interpretation of spatial and temporal patterns. Results will establish an important baseline for long-term monitoring and contribute to understanding microplastic pollution in protected marine ecosystems.

title: Flocculation-Based Removal of PVC (polyvinyl chloride), and Polyamide (PA) Microplastics Mixtures from Various Water Sources
description: Microplastics (MPs) pose a major global environmental challenge. We aim to utilize food-grade hydrophobic polymers (FGHP), recognized as safe (GRAS) materials, to effectively remove MPs from water. Our comparative case study will evaluate the removal efficiency of MPs, including PVC (polyvinyl chloride) and a polyamide (PA) mixture. We will test various water samples, nanopore, seawater, tap water, pond water, and biologically treated municipal wastewater, at room temperature. We will confirm the polymer type by FTIRµ. The MPs, ranging from 1µm to 5mm, will undergo a flocculation process, and residual FGHP will be monitored using ICP-MP measurements.

title: Preparing and Measuring Protein Samples by Transmission Electron Microscopy
description: Proteins are a few nanometers in size and cannot be seen with a light microscope. This project will test how protein concentration and negative staining affect their appearance in conventional transmission electron microscope (TEM) images. The student will prepare samples on TEM grids, collect images with the mentor, and use ImageJ to measure particle size, number, clustering, and image contrast. The results will provide a practical method for preparing protein samples and support future work on interactions between proteins and gold nanoparticles.

title: Dissolved oxygen and the health of Appalachian streams and rivers
description: This project will connect with ongoing research using high-frequency dissolved oxygen sensors and other water quality data to (1) understand how land cover changes alter stream functions, including low-oxygen (hypoxic) conditions; (2) test the role of different pollutants in altering microbial carbon metabolism and oxygen consumption; and/or (3) use large datasets to understand current and future connections between drought, flooding, and freshwater dissolved oxygen dynamics.

title: Biomechanics of animals
description: Our lab studies how animals work from a biomechanical perspective. That means that we use fundamental tools of engineering, physics, and math to understand how an animal’s form relates to its function. Our main focus is on snakes and insects, but we also study other animals: for instance, we are currently trying to understand how flying squid jump out of the water and fly the air. We do lots of research on snakes, centered on flying snakes and their relatives: how do they fly through the air? How do they jump? What limits other snakes from gliding?

title: Purification of recombinant human proteins for biochemical and structural studies
description: Students will learn how to produce and purify recombinant proteins for biochemical and structural studies. They will gain hands-on experience with basic protein chemistry and laboratory techniques, including preparing solutions, expressing proteins in bacterial cells, using chromatography for protein purification, measuring protein concentration and purity, and analyzing proteins by SDS-PAGE. Students will also learn to use common laboratory equipment, maintain accurate records, and analyze experimental results. Purified proteins will be used to investigate how proteins interact with other molecules and biological membranes and how protein structure relates to biological function.

title: Generative Molecular Dynamics Simulations of Soft Matter and Biophysical Systems
description: Classical molecular dynamics (MD) models many-body systems via Newtonian mechanics. Generative AI offers a promising alternative: recasting classical equations of motion as learned generation rules (genMD). While preliminary success has been demonstrated on simple protein chains, critical foundational challenges persist—specifically, maintaining physical consistency with governing laws, generalizing beyond linear chains to complex architectures, and accurately capturing nonequilibrium dynamics. This project addresses these challenges to establish a rigorous, physically consistent foundation for genMD, expanding its applicability across broad chemical and biomolecular systems.

title: LLM Evaluation and Applications
description: This project provides students with hands-on experience in the evaluation and application of large language models (LLMs). Students will contribute to ongoing research projects involving the deployment and testing of LLM-based tools, structured comparisons of LLM capabilities across different tasks and domains, and applications of LLMs in educational settings. Activities may include configuring existing tools, developing small supporting components, collecting and organizing evaluation data, comparing LLM outputs using defined criteria, and documenting findings. Students will work collaboratively under faculty supervision while developing practical skills in LLM evaluation, deployment, research documentation, and communication.

title: Southwest Virginia Language (SWVAL) Project
description: Even though it's at the point between a lot of interesting physical, political and dialectal borders, language patterns in Southwest Virginia are largely unstudied! We're fixing through a number of different data collection types, getting locals' opinions about language in the area, and also getting recordings of their speech, which we then process and analyze for features of interest!

title: Not Yet Replaceable? AI and Mentorship for Preservice Teachers
description: In the age of AI, with so much instant information available, do preservice music teachers still need mentorship from expert teachers, or can their questions be answered adequately using artificial intelligence? This research project will explore how AI may be helpful to preservice teachers at the undergraduate level and investigate the differences between what expert master teacher mentors have to offer and what can be accessed through AI. This research involves posing multi-faceted questions from preservice teachers to AI models and expert teachers and comparing the content of the answers, their nuance, and their perceived helpfulness.

title: How does temperature effect ticks that spread infectious diseases?
description: This project will explore how temperature impacts traits of ticks, and what this means for when and where we see ticks and the pathogens they spread. We will focus on tick species that are found in Virginia (e.g., Ixodes and Amblyomma ticks) that can spread a variety of diseases. We will primarily use published data and simple mathematical and statistical models.

title: VT Cube Satellite: Hack-a-Sat
description: VTNSI and Space@VT will design, build, test, launch, and operation of a next-generation Hack-a-Sat CubeSat Mission. Our preliminary design study demonstrates potential SWaP feasibility within a 6U CubeSat architecture. In addition to all legacy HAS, with Satellite Avionics Isolation, the design complements (1) hardware resource challenges and (2) inter-team hacking operations. Multiple cybersecurity environment features include: -Team-exclusive COTS boards (studied option: Raspberry Pi CM5 node). -Adaptive firmware or in-space reprogrammable boards (Linux Operating System and Application Layer). -Team-to-Team Hacking Arena through subsystem-isolated Ethernet LAN. -Extra-board Hack-a-Sat (Payload isolation) Hardware-Resource Competition, which includes cameras, servos, robotic arms, and more.

title: Hampton One Design and Chesapeake Maritime History
description: This research project will document the history of the Hampton One Design, a regional competitive watercraft sailed in the Chesapeake for nearly a century, and will contribute to the documentation of its materials, lines, and construction methods.

title: Engineering workforce development in the era of emerging technologies
description: Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, advanced manufacturing, and semiconductors are rapidly changing the skills, occupations, and workforce development strategies needed in engineering. This project examines how governments, industry organizations, and other stakeholders are responding to these changes through workforce policies, strategies, and initiatives. The student will support the research team by identifying, organizing, and analyzing workforce-related policy and strategy documents and helping identify patterns in how emerging technology workforce needs are defined and addressed.

description: Dogs experience the world through their noses, but which smells matter most to them? We bring an olfactometer, a device that delivers precise puffs of scent through three sniffing ports, right into dogs' homes, where they are comfortable. title: Can Electricity Program a Polymer? Exploring Field-Responsive Materials
description: What if we could use electricity to “program” plastics to behave differently? In this project, you will explore smart materials and future manufacturing by testing how electric fields can change the way polymers form and perform. You will make and compare materials with and without an electric field, then study how their properties change using imaging, mechanical testing, and other modern tools. The project connects to exciting areas such as programmable materials, responsive polymers, 3D printing, and next-generation technologies. No prior research experience is needed, just curiosity about how we can design the materials of the future.

title: Stories of Democracy: Children’s Literature and Historical Inquiry
description: What can a picture book tell us about American democracy, and how does its story compare with the historical record? This project examines how children’s literature can be paired with primary sources and music to support historical inquiry about topics such as equality, belonging, protest, citizenship, and social change. The undergraduate researcher will contribute to a larger collaborative project developing inquiry-based history resources for teachers. Depending on their interests, the student may investigate one historical inquiry in depth or help identify and evaluate literature across several inquiries.

title: Optimistic chickens: Does cooperative cognitive bias testing improve learning success?
description: Cognitive bias tests can be used to infer emotions in animals, including chickens. This project aims to determine whether learning success is impacted when chickens are tested individually or in pairs.

description: This project examines the role that attention plays in episodic memory in younger and older adults. The project explores what role attentional control plays in the benefits of different encoding strategies. Findings will contribute to our understanding of healthy cognitive aging and memory processes.

title: Smart Coalition: best practices and benchmark
description: Investigate through the world the existing best practices and benchmark in the architecture/construction industry on Smart Coalition. Specifically, find the top 10 universities leading this and understand why their lab/institute is so successful.

title: Understanding Thoughts and Feelings
description: Have you ever thought about the way you understand what is going on in someone else’s mind or your own? The ability to infer what people are thinking and feeling is important for our social relationships and mental health. Yet, despite its significance, we don’t understand what elements make up this skill or how it can affect our well-being. In this project, you will assist with collecting and processing data that will help us better understand how thinking about thoughts and feelings is related to mental illness.

title: Studying Changes in Human Strategy of Structural Knowledge Generalization
description: How do people extract abstract relational structure from experience and apply it to something entirely new? In this study, participants first learn how a small set of arbitrary symbols relate to one another through a hidden transition rule (e.g., which symbol "leads to" which, under different actions) — with no obvious spatial or visual logic to lean on. They are then given a new, larger set of unfamiliar symbols governed by the same hidden rule, and we test whether they can generalize without direct feedback. We'll use choice accuracy and reaction time to characterize how this abstract transfer unfolds, comparing behavior to predictions from a computational learning model.

title: Tracking Global Animal Disease Outbreaks and Their Impacts on Food and Agricultural Trade
description: Animal disease outbreaks—such as highly pathogenic avian influenza—disrupt food and agricultural markets worldwide: trading partners ban imports from affected regions, prices spike for consumers, and farmers lose export markets. This project builds a comprehensive database linking global animal disease outbreak events to the trade restrictions they trigger and the resulting market impacts. The student will help collect and organize outbreak reports, trade-ban announcements, and price data from public sources such as the World Organization for Animal Health and USDA. The database will support research on who bears the costs when disease shocks hit food markets.

title: Developing DiseaseSmart Conservation Program for Pollinators
description: This project will develop a disease-smart approach to pollinator conservation by integrating disease resistance, immune function, and population health into conservation planning. Using bumble bees as a model, the research will examine how to strengthen immune responses and incorporate them alongside existing approaches to support declining pollinator populations. The project will evaluate the feasibility, persistence, and potential consequences of enhancing disease resistance under ecologically relevant conditions. Ultimately, this work aims to establish a framework for integrating disease management with broader conservation strategies to improve the health and resilience of wild pollinator populations.

All of these projects are underpinned by the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with a focus on SDG #3: Good Health & Wellbeing, SDG #9: Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure, and SDG #10: Reduced Inequalities. Students will be assigned to one of these projects based on alignment with skills and interests.

title: Understanding Thoughts and Feelings
description: Have you ever thought about the way you understand what is going on in someone else’s mind or your own? The ability to infer what people are thinking and feeling is important for our social relationships and mental health. Yet, despite its significance, we don’t understand what elements make up this skill or how it can affect our well-being. In this project, you will assist with collecting and processing data that will help us better understand how thinking about thoughts and feelings is related to mental illness.

title: Southwest Virginia Language (SWVAL) Project
description: Even though it's at the point between a lot of interesting physical, political and dialectal borders, language patterns in Southwest Virginia are largely unstudied! We're fixing through a number of different data collection types, getting locals' opinions about language in the area, and also getting recordings of their speech, which we then process and analyze for features of interest!

title: Biomechanics of animals
description: Our lab studies how animals work from a biomechanical perspective. That means that we use fundamental tools of engineering, physics, and math to understand how an animal’s form relates to its function. Our main focus is on snakes and insects, but we also study other animals: for instance, we are currently trying to understand how flying squid jump out of the water and fly the air. We do lots of research on snakes, centered on flying snakes and their relatives: how do they fly through the air? How do they jump? What limits other snakes from gliding?

title: Optimistic chickens: Does cooperative cognitive bias testing improve learning success?
description: Cognitive bias tests can be used to infer emotions in animals, including chickens. A judgement bias test relates to optimism and relies on animals being trained to associate positive and negative cues with a reward and punishment. This training can be time-consuming and since chickens are social animals, it may be easier for them to learn discriminative tasks when with social support. This project aims to determine whether learning success is impacted when chickens are tested individually or in pairs.

title: Studying Changes in Human Strategy of Structural Knowledge Generalization
description: How do people extract abstract relational structure from experience and apply it to something entirely new? In this study, participants first learn how a small set of arbitrary symbols relate to one another through a hidden transition rule (e.g., which symbol "leads to" which, under different actions) — with no obvious spatial or visual logic to lean on. They are then given a new, larger set of unfamiliar symbols governed by the same hidden rule, and we test whether they can generalize without direct feedback. We'll use choice accuracy and reaction time to characterize how this abstract transfer unfolds, comparing behavior to predictions from a computational learning model.

title: Sniffari - Free Operant Investigation of Odors in Dogs
description: Dogs experience the world through their noses, but which smells matter most to them? We bring an olfactometer, a device that delivers precise puffs of scent through three sniffing ports, right into dogs' homes, where they are comfortable. Dogs are presented with odors from prey animals, familiar dogs, unfamiliar dogs, novel non-animal scents, and clean air. They are free to explore, and sensors record how long they sniff at each port. Each dog participates several times over a few weeks, revealing which odors remain interesting and fade, helping us understand what motivates dog sniffing behavior.

title: Not Yet Replaceable? AI and Mentorship for Preservice Teachers
description: In the age of AI, with so much instant information available, do preservice music teachers still need mentorship from expert teachers, or can their questions be answered adequately using artificial intelligence? This research project will explore how AI may be helpful to preservice teachers at the undergraduate level and investigate the differences between what expert master teacher mentors have to offer and what can be accessed through AI. This research involves posing multi-faceted questions from preservice teachers to AI models and expert teachers and comparing the content of the answers, their nuance, and their perceived helpfulness.

title: Nailed it: Exploring Effective Training for Nail Trims Using Scratch Boards
description: Nail trims, a necessary husbandry task, can be aversive for many dogs. Their responses suggest that the aversive quality of nail trims is not only a risk to the person trimming the nails but a welfare concern for the dogs. For nail trims, one cooperative option is using a scratchboard, where the dog scratches an abrasive board and trims its own nails in the process. This study assesses three training procedures used to teach dog owners how to train their dogs to use a scratchboard. We will examine the number of trials to criterion, frustration-related behaviors, and owner success.

title: Flocculation-Based Removal of PVC (polyvinyl chloride), and Polyamide (PA) Microplastics Mixtures from Various Water Sources
description: Microplastics (MPs) pose a major global environmental challenge. We aim to utilize food-grade hydrophobic polymers (FGHP), recognized as safe (GRAS) materials, to effectively remove MPs from water. Our comparative case study will evaluate the removal efficiency of MPs, including PVC (polyvinyl chloride) and a polyamide (PA) mixture. We will test various water samples, nanopore, seawater, tap water, pond water, and biologically treated municipal wastewater, at room temperature. We will confirm the polymer type by FTIRµ. The MPs, ranging from 1µm to 5mm, will undergo a flocculation process, and residual FGHP will be monitored using ICP-MP measurements.

title: Development of arbitrarily patterned patchy particles
description: In this bio-inspired project, the goal is to develop a new type of patchy particle, that is a particle where the surface is covered with patches that have different chemical and/or physical properties compared to the rest of the surface. The particles are intended to work as building blocks for self-assembly, that is the process where smaller components assemble into larger ordered structures, just like how proteins and other biomolecules self-assemble into anything from viral capsids to organelles, to cell membranes, to blood vessels.

title: Finding novel phages from the environment
description: Bacteriophages (phages) are viruses that specifically target bacteria. Often phages are of interest because of their ability to kill pathogenic bacteria, however they can also coexist with non-pathogenic bacteria including those that naturally reside in the gut microbiome. Little is known about the importance of these phages and a major limitation is that we have a limited availability of characterized phages that target these non-pathogenic bacteria.

title: VT Cube Satellite: Hack-a-Sat
description: VTNSI and Space@VT will design, build, test, launch, and operation of a next-generation Hack-a-Sat CubeSat Mission. Our preliminary design study demonstrates potential SWaP feasibility within a 6U CubeSat architecture. In addition to all legacy HAS, with Satellite Avionics Isolation, the design complements (1) hardware resource challenges and (2) inter-team hacking operations. Multiple cybersecurity environment features include: -Team-exclusive COTS boards (studied option: Raspberry Pi CM5 node). -Adaptive firmware or in-space reprogrammable boards (Linux Operating System and Application Layer). -Team-to-Team Hacking Arena through subsystem-isolated Ethernet LAN. -Extra-board Hack-a-Sat (Payload isolation) Hardware-Resource Competition, which includes cameras, servos, robotic arms, and more.

title: Stories of Democracy: Children’s Literature and Historical Inquiry
description: What can a picture book tell us about American democracy, and how does its story compare with the historical record? This project examines how children’s literature can be paired with primary sources and music to support historical inquiry about topics such as equality, belonging, protest, citizenship, and social change. The undergraduate researcher will contribute to a larger collaborative project developing inquiry-based history resources for teachers. Depending on their interests, the student may investigate one historical inquiry in depth or help identify and evaluate literature across several inquiries.

title: LLM Evaluation and Applications
description: This project provides students with hands-on experience in the evaluation and application of large language models (LLMs). Students will contribute to ongoing research projects involving the deployment and testing of LLM-based tools, structured comparisons of LLM capabilities across different tasks and domains, and applications of LLMs in educational settings. Activities may include configuring existing tools, developing small supporting components, collecting and organizing evaluation data, comparing LLM outputs using defined criteria, and documenting findings. Students will work collaboratively under faculty supervision while developing practical skills in LLM evaluation, deployment, research documentation, and communication.

title: Hampton One Design and Chesapeake Maritime History
description: This research project will document the history of the Hampton One Design, a regional competitive watercraft sailed in the Chesapeake for nearly a century, and will contribute to the documentation of its materials, lines, and construction methods.

title: University Archives Exploration
description: This project will jumpstart a larger initiative to identify legacy archival collections related to University History in Special Collections and University Archives' holdings. The student will review selected collections for their connection to the university's history with a brief report determining their potential for inclusion in the larger initiative. The report will be the culmination of the student's research of collections through collection finding aids (such as inventories and descriptions) and hands-on experience with archival materials. The student will also produce a blog post about their experience highlighting 1-3 collections they worked with.

title: Purification of recombinant human proteins for biochemical and structural studies
description: Students will learn how to produce and purify recombinant proteins for biochemical and structural studies. They will gain hands-on experience with basic protein chemistry and laboratory techniques, including preparing solutions, expressing proteins in bacterial cells, using chromatography for protein purification, measuring protein concentration and purity, and analyzing proteins by SDS-PAGE. Students will also learn to use common laboratory equipment, maintain accurate records, and analyze experimental results. Purified proteins will be used to investigate how proteins interact with other molecules and biological membranes and how protein structure relates to biological function.

description: The student will evaluate the effect of incubation length on the ruminal digestibility of feeds commonly fed to dairy cattle. Specifically, incubation periods of 240 and 288 hours will be compared to determine their influence on digestibility estimates. This research addresses a gap in the literature regarding the impact of extended incubation times on digestive measurements and will help improve the accuracy and consistency of feed evaluation methods used in dairy nutrition.

title: Preparing and Measuring Protein Samples by Transmission Electron Microscopy
description: Proteins are a few nanometers in size and cannot be seen with a light microscope. This project will test how protein concentration and negative staining affect their appearance in conventional transmission electron microscope (TEM) images. The student will prepare samples on TEM grids, collect images with the mentor, and use ImageJ to measure particle size, number, clustering, and image contrast. The results will provide a practical method for preparing protein samples and support future work on interactions between proteins and gold nanoparticles.

title: Can Electricity Program a Polymer? Exploring Field-Responsive Materials
description: What if we could use electricity to “program” plastics to behave differently? In this project, you will explore smart materials and future manufacturing by testing how electric fields can change the way polymers form and perform. You will make and compare materials with and without an electric field, then study how their properties change using imaging, mechanical testing, and other modern tools. The project connects to exciting areas such as programmable materials, responsive polymers, 3D printing, and next-generation technologies. No prior research experience is needed, just curiosity about how we can design the materials of the future.

This project builds a comprehensive database linking global animal disease outbreak events to the trade restrictions they trigger and the resulting market impacts. The student will help collect and organize outbreak reports, trade-ban announcements, and price data from public sources such as the World Organization for Animal Health and USDA. The database will support research on who bears the costs when disease shocks hit food markets.

title: How does temperature effect ticks that spread infectious diseases?
description: This project will explore how temperature impacts traits of ticks, and what this means for when and where we see ticks and the pathogens they spread. We will focus on tick species that are found in Virginia (e.g., Ixodes and Amblyomma ticks) that can spread a variety of diseases. We will primarily use published data and simple mathematical and statistical models.

title: Dissolved oxygen and the health of Appalachian streams and rivers
description: This project will connect with ongoing research using high-frequency dissolved oxygen sensors and other water quality data to (1) understand how land cover changes alter stream functions, including low-oxygen (hypoxic) conditions; (2) test the role of different pollutants in altering microbial carbon metabolism and oxygen consumption; and/or (3) use large datasets to understand current and future connections between drought, flooding, and freshwater dissolved oxygen dynamics.

title: Determining the First Amino Acid Sequence of Proteins Unencoded By The Genome
description: When a ribosome stalls, a quality-control system extends the trapped protein with "CAT tails" — amino acids added with no genetic template. Because these sequences come from no gene and appear as heterogeneous smears, none has ever been sequenced, and no antibody against them exists. Using a reporter we engineered to make CAT tails of a single, defined length, this project will purify these tails from yeast and determine their amino acid sequence for the first time. That sequence will let us build the first anti-CAT-tail antibody and identify the proteins cells naturally tail.

title: Smart Coalition: best practices and benchmark
description: Investigate through the world the existing best practices and benchmark in the architecture/construction industry on Smart Coalition. Specifically, find the top 10 universities leading this and understand why their lab/institute is so successful.

title: Generative Molecular Dynamics Simulations of Soft Matter and Biophysical Systems
description: Classical molecular dynamics (MD) models many-body systems via Newtonian mechanics. Generative AI offers a promising alternative: recasting classical equations of motion as learned generation rules (genMD). While preliminary success has been demonstrated on simple protein chains, critical foundational challenges persist—specifically, maintaining physical consistency with governing laws, generalizing beyond linear chains to complex architectures, and accurately capturing nonequilibrium dynamics. This project addresses these challenges to establish a rigorous, physically consistent foundation for genMD, expanding its applicability across broad chemical and biomolecular systems.

title: Exploring Encoding Strategies, Attention, and Memory in Aging Adults
description: This project examines the role that attention plays in episodic memory in younger and older adults. Participants study words under conditions that vary in the type of encoding questions they answer while multitasking. They are later tested with either matching or non-matching questions. The project explores what role attentional control plays in the benefits of different encoding strategies. Findings will contribute to our understanding of healthy cognitive aging and memory processes.

title: Screening push-pull strategy companion plants as secondary hosts for major brassica pests in Virginia
description: Push-pull strategies (PPS) are a companion planting approach that manipulates insect behavior for pest management. The push plant repels the pest from the cash crop, while the pull plant draws the pest to another location where they can be more effectively controlled. This management can be the use of additional pull plants that attract beneficial insects to kill the pests. Careful selection of PPS plants is critical, as some may serve as secondary hosts and inadvertently increase pest abundance. This study evaluates PPS plants to determine whether pests of concern in collard production can use them as secondary hosts.

title: Engineering workforce development in the era of emerging technologies
description: Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, advanced manufacturing, and semiconductors are rapidly changing the skills, occupations, and workforce development strategies needed in engineering. This project examines how governments, industry organizations, and other stakeholders are responding to these changes through workforce policies, strategies, and initiatives. The student will support the research team by identifying, organizing, and analyzing workforce-related policy and strategy documents and helping identify patterns in how emerging technology workforce needs are defined and addressed.

title: Developing DiseaseSmart Conservation Program for Pollinators
description: This project will develop a disease-smart approach to pollinator conservation by integrating disease resistance, immune function, and population health into conservation planning. title: Using CRISPR to modify the genome of the human fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans
description: The focus of the lab is to understand how the pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans is able to infect, survive, and cause disease in mammalian hosts such as humans. One mechanism we utilize is gene editing in Cryptococcus using CRISPR technology.

title: Using Metagenomics to Detect and Identify Pathogens Affecting Plant and Animal Health
description: This project introduces students to the use of metagenomics and genomic technologies for identifying pathogens associated with plant and animal diseases. The student will work with the research team at Virginia Tech’s (Meta)Genomics-Based Pathogen Identification Center for Animal and Plant Disease Diagnostics, Biosecurity, and Pandemic Prevention to explore how DNA and RNA sequencing can detect bacteria, fungi, viruses, and other microorganisms directly from biological samples. Depending on the project stage, activities may include sample and data organization, basic laboratory procedures such as nucleic acid extractions, sequencing library preparation and sequencing. The student will gain hands-on experience with modern approaches used in metagenomics disease diagnostics, surveillance, and pathogen discovery.

title: Finding novel phages from the environment
description: Bacteriophages (phages) are viruses that specifically target bacteria. Little is known about the importance of these phages and a major limitation is that we have a limited availability of characterized phages that target these non-pathogenic bacteria.

title: Determining the First Amino Acid Sequence of Proteins Unencoded By The Genome
description: When a ribosome stalls, a quality-control system extends the trapped protein with "CAT tails" — amino acids added with no genetic template. title: Genetics of Hybrid Male Sterility in Malaria Mosquitoes
description: The project seeks to explore the genetic basis of reproductive isolation between closely related species of Anopheles, the genus of mosquitoes responsible for transmitting malaria. We will test this hypothesis by mapping the genomic regions responsible for hybrid male sterility in crosses between Anopheles gambiae and An. merus.

title: Bacteriophages of the soybean symbiont Bradyrhizobium diazoefficiens

We will isolate B. diazoefficiens phages from soybean nodules and characterize their interaction with their host.

description: Students will learn how to produce and purify recombinant proteins for biochemical and structural studies. Purified proteins will be used to investigate how proteins interact with other molecules and biological membranes and how protein structure relates to biological function.

title: Flocculation-Based Removal of PVC (polyvinyl chloride), and Polyamide (PA) Microplastics Mixtures from Various Water Sources
description: Microplastics (MPs) pose a major global environmental challenge. Our comparative case study will evaluate the removal efficiency of MPs, including PVC (polyvinyl chloride) and a polyamide (PA) mixture. We will test various water samples, nanopore, seawater, tap water, pond water, and biologically treated municipal wastewater, at room temperature. We will confirm the polymer type by FTIRµ. title: Dissolved oxygen and the health of Appalachian streams and rivers
description: This project will connect with ongoing research using high-frequency dissolved oxygen sensors and other water quality data to (1) understand how land cover changes alter stream functions, including low-oxygen (hypoxic) conditions; (2) test the role of different pollutants in altering microbial carbon metabolism and oxygen consumption; and/or (3) use large datasets to understand current and future connections between drought, flooding, and freshwater dissolved oxygen dynamics.

title: Can Electricity Program a Polymer? Exploring Field-Responsive Materials
description: What if we could use electricity to “program” plastics to behave differently? You will make and compare materials with and without an electric field, then study how their properties change using imaging, mechanical testing, and other modern tools. The project connects to exciting areas such as programmable materials, responsive polymers, 3D printing, and next-generation technologies. No prior research experience is needed, just curiosity about how we can design the materials of the future.

title: From Waste Rock to Architectural Surfaces: Valorizing Appalachian Shale
description: Excavation for roads, buildings, and mining operations across our region generates large volumes of shale rock, some stockpiled, but much of it already used for lower-value engineering purposes such as temporary roads, staging areas, and backfill. This project investigates whether that same material can instead be diverted toward higher-value architectural surfaces, such as countertops, tile, and decorative panels, much as recycled glass became the basis for today's terrazzo countertop industry. Research students will help characterize samples, test preparation methods, and explore possible finished products, while questioning what makes some shale visually striking and other shale unremarkable.

description: This project provides students with hands-on experience in the evaluation and application of large language models (LLMs). Activities may include configuring existing tools, developing small supporting components, collecting and organizing evaluation data, comparing LLM outputs using defined criteria, and documenting findings. Students will work collaboratively under faculty supervision while developing practical skills in LLM evaluation, deployment, research documentation, and communication.

title: Southwest Virginia Language (SWVAL) Project
description: Even though it's at the point between a lot of interesting physical, political and dialectal borders, language patterns in Southwest Virginia are largely unstudied! We're fixing through a number of different data collection types, getting locals' opinions about language in the area, and also getting recordings of their speech, which we then process and analyze for features of interest!

title: Syntactical Architecture
description: Architectural documentation/drawing/layout/library research for a new book project titled "Syntactical Architecture."

title: VT Cube Satellite: Hack-a-Sat
description: VTNSI and Space@VT will design, build, test, launch, and operation of a next-generation Hack-a-Sat CubeSat Mission. Our preliminary design study demonstrates potential SWaP feasibility within a 6U CubeSat architecture. In addition to all legacy HAS, with Satellite Avionics Isolation, the design complements (1) hardware resource challenges and (2) inter-team hacking operations. Multiple cybersecurity environment features include: -Team-exclusive COTS boards (studied option: Raspberry Pi CM5 node). -Adaptive firmware or in-space reprogrammable boards (Linux Operating System and Application Layer). -Team-to-Team Hacking Arena through subsystem-isolated Ethernet LAN. -Extra-board Hack-a-Sat (Payload isolation) Hardware-Resource Competition, which includes cameras, servos, robotic arms, and more.

title: TEAM Malawi
description: Students enrolled in this section of IDS 4994 will leverage the Biodesign Process (Figure 1, below) to identify and invent solutions to high-priority projects in sub-Saharan Africa. All of these projects are underpinned by the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with a focus on SDG #3: Good Health & Wellbeing, SDG #9: Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure, and SDG #10: Reduced Inequalities. Students will be assigned to one of these projects based on alignment with skills and interests.

title: Hampton One Design and Chesapeake Maritime History
description: This research project will document the history of the Hampton One Design, a regional competitive watercraft sailed in the Chesapeake for nearly a century, and will contribute to the documentation of its materials, lines, and construction methods.

title: Smart Coalition: best practices and benchmark
description: Investigate through the world the existing best practices and benchmark in the architecture/construction industry on Smart Coalition. Specifically, find the top 10 universities leading this and understand why their lab/institute is so successful.

title: Biomechanics of animals
description: Our lab studies how animals work from a biomechanical perspective. That means that we use fundamental tools of engineering, physics, and math to understand how an animal’s form relates to its function. Our main focus is on snakes and insects, but we also study other animals: for instance, we are currently trying to understand how flying squid jump out of the water and fly the air. We do lots of research on snakes, centered on flying snakes and their relatives: how do they fly through the air? How do they jump? What limits other snakes from gliding?

title: Nailed it: Exploring Effective Training for Nail Trims Using Scratch Boards
description: Nail trims, a necessary husbandry task, can be aversive for many dogs. Their responses suggest that the aversive quality of nail trims is not only a risk to the person trimming the nails but a welfare concern for the dogs. For nail trims, one cooperative option is using a scratchboard, where the dog scratches an abrasive board and trims its own nails in the process. This study assesses three training procedures used to teach dog owners how to train their dogs to use a scratchboard. We will examine the number of trials to criterion, frustration-related behaviors, and owner success.

title: Sniffari - Free Operant Investigation of Odors in Dogs
description: Dogs experience the world through their noses, but which smells matter most to them? We bring an olfactometer, a device that delivers precise puffs of scent through three sniffing ports, right into dogs' homes, where they are comfortable. Dogs are presented with odors from prey animals, familiar dogs, unfamiliar dogs, novel non-animal scents, and clean air. They are free to explore, and sensors record how long they sniff at each port. Each dog participates several times over a few weeks, revealing which odors remain interesting and fade, helping us understand what motivates dog sniffing behavior.

title: Development of arbitrarily patterned patchy particles
description: In this bio-inspired project, the goal is to develop a new type of patchy particle, that is a particle where the surface is covered with patches that have different chemical and/or physical properties compared to the rest of the surface. The particles are intended to work as building blocks for self-assembly, that is the process where smaller components assemble into larger ordered structures, just like how proteins and other biomolecules self-assemble into anything from viral capsids to organelles, to cell membranes, to blood vessels.

description: Have you ever thought about the way you understand what is going on in someone else’s mind or your own? Yet, despite its significance, we don’t understand what elements make up this skill or how it can affect our well-being. In this project, you will assist with collecting and processing data that will help us better understand how thinking about thoughts and feelings is related to mental illness.

The project explores what role attentional control plays in the benefits of different encoding strategies. Findings will contribute to our understanding of healthy cognitive aging and memory processes.

title: Examining the variation of microplastic type and abundance over seasons and sites within Watamu Marine National Park and Reserve, Kenya
description: Microplastic pollution is an increasing threat to marine ecosystems, yet little is known about contamination in protected coastal areas of Kenya. This project provides the first assessment of microplastic abundance and composition along sandy shorelines within Watamu Marine National Park. Samples were collected across five sampling periods in 2021–2022 using standardized transect and quadrat methods, and microplastics were extracted, classified, measured, and enumerated. The student will help complete data organization, quality control, statistical analyses, and interpretation of spatial and temporal patterns. Results will establish an important baseline for long-term monitoring and contribute to understanding microplastic pollution in protected marine ecosystems.

title: Biomechanics of animals
description: Our lab studies how animals work from a biomechanical perspective. That means that we use fundamental tools of engineering, physics, and math to understand how an animal’s form relates to its function. Our main focus is on snakes and insects, but we also study other animals: for instance, we are currently trying to understand how flying squid jump out of the water and fly the air. We do lots of research on snakes, centered on flying snakes and their relatives: how do they fly through the air? How do they jump? What limits other snakes from gliding?

title: Nailed it: Exploring Effective Training for Nail Trims Using Scratch Boards
description: Nail trims, a necessary husbandry task, can be aversive for many dogs. Their responses suggest that the aversive quality of nail trims is not only a risk to the person trimming the nails but a welfare concern for the dogs. For nail trims, one cooperative option is using a scratchboard, where the dog scratches an abrasive board and trims its own nails in the process. This study assesses three training procedures used to teach dog owners how to train their dogs to use a scratchboard. We will examine the number of trials to criterion, frustration-related behaviors, and owner success.

title: Sniffari - Free Operant Investigation of Odors in Dogs
description: Dogs experience the world through their noses, but which smells matter most to them? We bring an olfactometer, a device that delivers precise puffs of scent through three sniffing ports, right into dogs' homes, where they are comfortable. Dogs are presented with odors from prey animals, familiar dogs, unfamiliar dogs, novel non-animal scents, and clean air. They are free to explore, and sensors record how long they sniff at each port. Each dog participates several times over a few weeks, revealing which odors remain interesting and fade, helping us understand what motivates dog sniffing behavior.

title: Developing DiseaseSmart Conservation Program for Pollinators
description: This project will develop a disease-smart approach to pollinator conservation by integrating disease resistance, immune function, and population health into conservation planning. Using bumble bees as a model, the research will examine how to strengthen immune responses and incorporate them alongside existing approaches to support declining pollinator populations. The project will evaluate the feasibility, persistence, and potential consequences of enhancing disease resistance under ecologically relevant conditions. Ultimately, this work aims to establish a framework for integrating disease management with broader conservation strategies to improve the health and resilience of wild pollinator populations.

title: Optimistic chickens: Does cooperative cognitive bias testing improve learning success?
description: Cognitive bias tests can be used to infer emotions in animals, including chickens. A judgement bias test relates to optimism and relies on animals being trained to associate positive and negative cues with a reward and punishment. This training can be time-consuming and since chickens are social animals, it may be easier for them to learn discriminative tasks when with social support. This project aims to determine whether learning success is impacted when chickens are tested individually or in pairs.

title: Tracking Global Animal Disease Outbreaks and Their Impacts on Food and Agricultural Trade
description: Animal disease outbreaks—such as highly pathogenic avian influenza—disrupt food and agricultural markets worldwide: trading partners ban imports from affected regions, prices spike for consumers, and farmers lose export markets. This project builds a comprehensive database linking global animal disease outbreak events to the trade restrictions they trigger and the resulting market impacts. The student will help collect and organize outbreak reports, trade-ban announcements, and price data from public sources such as the World Organization for Animal Health and USDA. The database will support research on who bears the costs when disease shocks hit food markets.

title: Understanding Thoughts and Feelings
description: Have you ever thought about the way you understand what is going on in someone else’s mind or your own? The ability to infer what people are thinking and feeling is important for our social relationships and mental health. Yet, despite its significance, we don’t understand what elements make up this skill or how it can affect our well-being. In this project, you will assist with collecting and processing data that will help us better understand how thinking about thoughts and feelings is related to mental illness.

title: Finding novel phages from the environment
description: Bacteriophages (phages) are viruses that specifically target bacteria. Often phages are of interest because of their ability to kill pathogenic bacteria, however they can also coexist with non-pathogenic bacteria including those that naturally reside in the gut microbiome. Little is known about the importance of these phages and a major limitation is that we have a limited availability of characterized phages that target these non-pathogenic bacteria.

description: Students enrolled in this section of IDS 4994 will leverage the Biodesign Process (Figure 1, below) to identify and invent solutions to high-priority projects in sub-Saharan Africa. Students will be assigned to one of these projects based on alignment with skills and interests.

title: From Waste Rock to Architectural Surfaces: Valorizing Appalachian Shale
description: Excavation for roads, buildings, and mining operations across our region generates large volumes of shale rock, some stockpiled, but much of it already used for lower-value engineering purposes such as temporary roads, staging areas, and backfill. This project investigates whether that same material can instead be diverted toward higher-value architectural surfaces, such as countertops, tile, and decorative panels, much as recycled glass became the basis for today's terrazzo countertop industry. Research students will help characterize samples, test preparation methods, and explore possible finished products, while questioning what makes some shale visually striking and other shale unremarkable.

The undergraduate researcher will contribute to a larger collaborative project developing inquiry-based history resources for teachers. title: Studying Changes in Human Strategy of Structural Knowledge Generalization
description: How do people extract abstract relational structure from experience and apply it to something entirely new? In this study, participants first learn how a small set of arbitrary symbols relate to one another through a hidden transition rule (e.g., which symbol "leads to" which, under different actions) — with no obvious spatial or visual logic to lean on. They are then given a new, larger set of unfamiliar symbols governed by the same hidden rule, and we test whether they can generalize without direct feedback. We'll use choice accuracy and reaction time to characterize how this abstract transfer unfolds, comparing behavior to predictions from a computational learning model.

title: Not Yet Replaceable? AI and Mentorship for Preservice Teachers
description: In the age of AI, with so much instant information available, do preservice music teachers still need mentorship from expert teachers, or can their questions be answered adequately using artificial intelligence? This research project will explore how AI may be helpful to preservice teachers at the undergraduate level and investigate the differences between what expert master teacher mentors have to offer and what can be accessed through AI. This research involves posing multi-faceted questions from preservice teachers to AI models and expert teachers and comparing the content of the answers, their nuance, and their perceived helpfulness.

title: LLM Evaluation and Applications
description: This project provides students with hands-on experience in the evaluation and application of large language models (LLMs). Activities may include configuring existing tools, developing small supporting components, collecting and organizing evaluation data, comparing LLM outputs using defined criteria, and documenting findings. Students will work collaboratively under faculty supervision while developing practical skills in LLM evaluation, deployment, research documentation, and communication.

title: Abuse Prevention Education and Societal Bias
description: Children with intellectual and developmental disabilities are at increased risk of sexual abuse, yet often receive limited access to prevention education. In the U.S., sexual education is not universal and is often stigmatized; children with disabilities may be excluded from sexual education and safety programs. This project examines results of an online survey; participants responded on appropriateness of National Sex Education Standards items labeled as “sexual education,” “health education,” or unlabeled, along with measures of morality, disgust, and warmth/competence, determining adult support for identical prevention content depending on label attached and whether the child is described as having a disability.

title: Preparing and Measuring Protein Samples by Transmission Electron Microscopy
description: Proteins are a few nanometers in size and cannot be seen with a light microscope. The results will provide a practical method for preparing protein samples and support future work on interactions between proteins and gold nanoparticles.

title: Development of arbitrarily patterned patchy particles
description: In this bio-inspired project, the goal is to develop a new type of patchy particle, that is a particle where the surface is covered with patches that have different chemical and/or physical properties compared to the rest of the surface. title: VT Cube Satellite: Hack-a-Sat
description: VTNSI and Space@VT will design, build, test, launch, and operation of a next-generation Hack-a-Sat CubeSat Mission. Our preliminary design study demonstrates potential SWaP feasibility within a 6U CubeSat architecture. In addition to all legacy HAS, with Satellite Avionics Isolation, the design complements (1) hardware resource challenges and (2) inter-team hacking operations. Depending on the project stage, activities may include sample and data organization, basic laboratory procedures such as nucleic acid extractions, sequencing library preparation and sequencing. The student will gain hands-on experience with modern approaches used in metagenomics disease diagnostics, surveillance, and pathogen discovery.

title: Determining the First Amino Acid Sequence of Proteins Unencoded By The Genome
description: When a ribosome stalls, a quality-control system extends the trapped protein with "CAT tails" — amino acids added with no genetic template. Because these sequences come from no gene and appear as heterogeneous smears, none has ever been sequenced, and no antibody against them exists. Using a reporter we engineered to make CAT tails of a single, defined length, this project will purify these tails from yeast and determine their amino acid sequence for the first time. That sequence will let us build the first anti-CAT-tail antibody and identify the proteins cells naturally tail.

title: How much does vacuum pressure impact destruction of pathogens during sous vide cooking?
description: Sous vide is the cooking of vacuum packaged meat in a water bath. It has become increasingly popular with the availability and affordability of home cook-level heating devices. However, there is a big difference between meat that is commercially vacuum sealed, and meat placed into a storage bag and squeezing out the air, and it may have implications on the ability to control foodborne pathogens. Potentially, cooking without the benefit of vacuum sealing may change the relative lethality of sous vide cooking, but there is just no data to suggest if, or to what extent, this may be true.

title: Ticks as vectors of disease
description: Assessment of ticks as vector for One Health pathogens of disease

title: Bacteriophages of the soybean symbiont Bradyrhizobium diazoefficiens
description: Soybean is an important crop and the most common source for vegetable oil. The symbiotic bacterium Bradyrhizobium diazoefficiens is found in leguminous root nodules, where it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and ultimately stimulates soybean growth. Bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria, are the most abundant biological entity on earth and important factors in shaping ecosystems including during bacteria-host interactions. However, very little is known about bacteriophages infecting symbiotic rhizobia. This is particularly true for the soybean symbiont and only a few Bradyrhizobium phages have been described. We will isolate B. diazoefficiens phages from soybean nodules and characterize their interaction with their host.

title: Finding novel phages from the environment
description: Bacteriophages (phages) are viruses that specifically target bacteria. Often phages are of interest because of their ability to kill pathogenic bacteria, however they can also coexist with non-pathogenic bacteria including those that naturally reside in the gut microbiome. Little is known about the importance of these phages and a major limitation is that we have a limited availability of characterized phages that target these non-pathogenic bacteria.

title: Using CRISPR to modify the genome of the human fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans
description: The focus of the lab is to understand how the pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans is able to infect, survive, and cause disease in mammalian hosts such as humans. One mechanism we utilize is gene editing in Cryptococcus using CRISPR technology.

title: Purification of recombinant human proteins for biochemical and structural studies
description: Students will learn how to produce and purify recombinant proteins for biochemical and structural studies. They will gain hands-on experience with basic protein chemistry and laboratory techniques, including preparing solutions, expressing proteins in bacterial cells, using chromatography for protein purification, measuring protein concentration and purity, and analyzing proteins by SDS-PAGE. Students will also learn to use common laboratory equipment, maintain accurate records, and analyze experimental results. Purified proteins will be used to investigate how proteins interact with other molecules and biological membranes and how protein structure relates to biological function.

title: Examining the variation of microplastic type and abundance over seasons and sites within Watamu Marine National Park and Reserve, Kenya
description: Microplastic pollution is an increasing threat to marine ecosystems, yet little is known about contamination in protected coastal areas of Kenya. This project provides the first assessment of microplastic abundance and composition along sandy shorelines within Watamu Marine National Park. Samples were collected across five sampling periods in 2021–2022 using standardized transect and quadrat methods, and microplastics were extracted, classified, measured, and enumerated. The student will help complete data organization, quality control, statistical analyses, and interpretation of spatial and temporal patterns. Results will establish an important baseline for long-term monitoring and contribute to understanding microplastic pollution in protected marine ecosystems.

title: Flocculation-Based Removal of PVC (polyvinyl chloride), and Polyamide (PA) Microplastics Mixtures from Various Water Sources
description: Microplastics (MPs) pose a major global environmental challenge. We aim to utilize food-grade hydrophobic polymers (FGHP), recognized as safe (GRAS) materials, to effectively remove MPs from water. Our comparative case study will evaluate the removal efficiency of MPs, including PVC (polyvinyl chloride) and a polyamide (PA) mixture. We will test various water samples, nanopore, seawater, tap water, pond water, and biologically treated municipal wastewater, at room temperature. We will confirm the polymer type by FTIRµ. The MPs, ranging from 1µm to 5mm, will undergo a flocculation process, and residual FGHP will be monitored using ICP-MP measurements.

title: Dissolved oxygen and the health of Appalachian streams and rivers
description: This project will connect with ongoing research using high-frequency dissolved oxygen sensors and other water quality data to (1) understand how land cover changes alter stream functions, including low-oxygen (hypoxic) conditions; (2) test the role of different pollutants in altering microbial carbon metabolism and oxygen consumption; and/or (3) use large datasets to understand current and future connections between drought, flooding, and freshwater dissolved oxygen dynamics.

title: Preparing and Measuring Protein Samples by Transmission Electron Microscopy
description: Proteins are a few nanometers in size and cannot be seen with a light microscope. This project will test how protein concentration and negative staining affect their appearance in conventional transmission electron microscope (TEM) images. The student will prepare samples on TEM grids, collect images with the mentor, and use ImageJ to measure particle size, number, clustering, and image contrast. The results will provide a practical method for preparing protein samples and support future work on interactions between proteins and gold nanoparticles.

title: From Waste Rock to Architectural Surfaces: Valorizing Appalachian Shale
description: Excavation for roads, buildings, and mining operations across our region generates large volumes of shale rock, some stockpiled, but much of it already used for lower-value engineering purposes such as temporary roads, staging areas, and backfill. This project investigates whether that same material can instead be diverted toward higher-value architectural surfaces, such as countertops, tile, and decorative panels, much as recycled glass became the basis for today's terrazzo countertop industry. Research students will help characterize samples, test preparation methods, and explore possible finished products, while questioning what makes some shale visually striking and other shale unremarkable.

title: Generative Molecular Dynamics Simulations of Soft Matter and Biophysical Systems
description: Classical molecular dynamics (MD) models many-body systems via Newtonian mechanics. Generative AI offers a promising alternative: recasting classical equations of motion as learned generation rules (genMD). This project addresses these challenges to establish a rigorous, physically consistent foundation for genMD, expanding its applicability across broad chemical and biomolecular systems.

title: LLM Evaluation and Applications
description: This project provides students with hands-on experience in the evaluation and application of large language models (LLMs). Students will contribute to ongoing research projects involving the deployment and testing of LLM-based tools, structured comparisons of LLM capabilities across different tasks and domains, and applications of LLMs in educational settings. Activities may include configuring existing tools, developing small supporting components, collecting and organizing evaluation data, comparing LLM outputs using defined criteria, and documenting findings. Students will work collaboratively under faculty supervision while developing practical skills in LLM evaluation, deployment, research documentation, and communication.

title: Southwest Virginia Language (SWVAL) Project
description: Even though it's at the point between a lot of interesting physical, political and dialectal borders, language patterns in Southwest Virginia are largely unstudied! We're fixing through a number of different data collection types, getting locals' opinions about language in the area, and also getting recordings of their speech, which we then process and analyze for features of interest!

title: Not Yet Replaceable? AI and Mentorship for Preservice Teachers
description: In the age of AI, with so much instant information available, do preservice music teachers still need mentorship from expert teachers, or can their questions be answered adequately using artificial intelligence? This research project will explore how AI may be helpful to preservice teachers at the undergraduate level and investigate the differences between what expert master teacher mentors have to offer and what can be accessed through AI. This research involves posing multi-faceted questions from preservice teachers to AI models and expert teachers and comparing the content of the answers, their nuance, and their perceived helpfulness.

title: Studying Changes in Human Strategy of Structural Knowledge Generalization
description: How do people extract abstract relational structure from experience and apply it to something entirely new? title: VT Cube Satellite: Hack-a-Sat
description: VTNSI and Space@VT will design, build, test, launch, and operation of a next-generation Hack-a-Sat CubeSat Mission. Our preliminary design study demonstrates potential SWaP feasibility within a 6U CubeSat architecture. In addition to all legacy HAS, with Satellite Avionics Isolation, the design complements (1) hardware resource challenges and (2) inter-team hacking operations. Multiple cybersecurity environment features include: -Team-exclusive COTS boards (studied option: Raspberry Pi CM5 node). -Adaptive firmware or in-space reprogrammable boards (Linux Operating System and Application Layer). -Team-to-Team Hacking Arena through subsystem-isolated Ethernet LAN. -Extra-board Hack-a-Sat (Payload isolation) Hardware-Resource Competition, which includes cameras, servos, robotic arms, and more.

title: Hampton One Design and Chesapeake Maritime History
description: This research project will document the history of the Hampton One Design, a regional competitive watercraft sailed in the Chesapeake for nearly a century, and will contribute to the documentation of its materials, lines, and construction methods.

title: Sniffari - Free Operant Investigation of Odors in Dogs
description: Dogs experience the world through their noses, but which smells matter most to them? We bring an olfactometer, a device that delivers precise puffs of scent through three sniffing ports, right into dogs' homes, where they are comfortable. Dogs are presented with odors from prey animals, familiar dogs, unfamiliar dogs, novel non-animal scents, and clean air. They are free to explore, and sensors record how long they sniff at each port. Each dog participates several times over a few weeks, revealing which odors remain interesting and fade, helping us understand what motivates dog sniffing behavior.

title: Biomechanics of animals
description: Our lab studies how animals work from a biomechanical perspective. That means that we use fundamental tools of engineering, physics, and math to understand how an animal’s form relates to its function. Our main focus is on snakes and insects, but we also study other animals: for instance, we are currently trying to understand how flying squid jump out of the water and fly the air. We do lots of research on snakes, centered on flying snakes and their relatives: how do they fly through the air? How do they jump? What limits other snakes from gliding?

title: Can Electricity Program a Polymer? Exploring Field-Responsive Materials
description: What if we could use electricity to “program” plastics to behave differently? In this project, you will explore smart materials and future manufacturing by testing how electric fields can change the way polymers form and perform. You will make and compare materials with and without an electric field, then study how their properties change using imaging, mechanical testing, and other modern tools. The project connects to exciting areas such as programmable materials, responsive polymers, 3D printing, and next-generation technologies. No prior research experience is needed, just curiosity about how we can design the materials of the future.

title: Nailed it: Exploring Effective Training for Nail Trims Using Scratch Boards
description: Nail trims, a necessary husbandry task, can be aversive for many dogs. Their responses suggest that the aversive quality of nail trims is not only a risk to the person trimming the nails but a welfare concern for the dogs. For nail trims, one cooperative option is using a scratchboard, where the dog scratches an abrasive board and trims its own nails in the process. This study assesses three training procedures used to teach dog owners how to train their dogs to use a scratchboard. We will examine the number of trials to criterion, frustration-related behaviors, and owner success.

title: Optimistic chickens: Does cooperative cognitive bias testing improve learning success?
description: Cognitive bias tests can be used to infer emotions in animals, including chickens. A judgement bias test relates to optimism and relies on animals being trained to associate positive and negative cues with a reward and punishment. This training can be time-consuming and since chickens are social animals, it may be easier for them to learn discriminative tasks when with social support. This project aims to determine whether learning success is impacted when chickens are tested individually or in pairs.

title: How does temperature effect ticks that spread infectious diseases?
description: This project will explore how temperature impacts traits of ticks, and what this means for when and where we see ticks and the pathogens they spread. We will focus on tick species that are found in Virginia (e.g., Ixodes and Amblyomma ticks) that can spread a variety of diseases. We will primarily use published data and simple mathematical and statistical models.

title: Tracking Global Animal Disease Outbreaks and Their Impacts on Food and Agricultural Trade
description: Animal disease outbreaks—such as highly pathogenic avian influenza—disrupt food and agricultural markets worldwide: trading partners ban imports from affected regions, prices spike for consumers, and farmers lose export markets. This project builds a comprehensive database linking global animal disease outbreak events to the trade restrictions they trigger and the resulting market impacts. The student will help collect and organize outbreak reports, trade-ban announcements, and price data from public sources such as the World Organization for Animal Health and USDA. The database will support research on who bears the costs when disease shocks hit food markets.

The project explores what role attentional control plays in the benefits of different encoding strategies. Findings will contribute to our understanding of healthy cognitive aging and memory processes.

description: Investigate through the world the existing best practices and benchmark in the architecture/construction industry on Smart Coalition. Specifically, find the top 10 universities leading this and understand why their lab/institute is so successful.

title: Understanding Thoughts and Feelings
description: Have you ever thought about the way you understand what is going on in someone else’s mind or your own? The ability to infer what people are thinking and feeling is important for our social relationships and mental health. Yet, despite its significance, we don’t understand what elements make up this skill or how it can affect our well-being. In this project, you will assist with collecting and processing data that will help us better understand how thinking about thoughts and feelings is related to mental illness.

The undergraduate researcher will contribute to a larger collaborative project developing inquiry-based history resources around themes such as equality, protest, citizenship, belonging, labor, and social change. Depending on their interests, the student may investigate one song and its historical context in depth or work across several inquiries to locate, evaluate, and organize relevant primary sources from digital archives.

Ultimately, this work aims to establish a framework for integrating disease management with broader conservation strategies to improve the health and resilience of wild pollinator populations.

description: In this bio-inspired project, the goal is to develop a new type of patchy particle, that is a particle where the surface is covered with patches that have different chemical and/or physical properties compared to the rest of the surface.
